title: His death, 1839
hook: when he died, several queens and servants burned on his pyre, against the Gurus' teaching

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maharani Jind Kaur, and your line was a brave queen. Which brave mother did you honor? Today is a heavy day. Go gently with it. Day nine hundred twenty-five.

The man who built the kingdom is old now. Strokes have taken much of his speech. In his last days, tradition says, he gave away gifts and treasure, and his court gathered around him in Lahore. Then the Lion of the Punjab died, and the city mourned. What happened at his funeral is part of this story, and Sikh histories tell it honestly, because the Gurus had already spoken to it. Today: his death.
screen: `THE MAHARAJA GROWS OLD.` → `HIS COURT GATHERS IN LAHORE.` → `THE LION OF THE PUNJAB DIES.`

segments.voice: First, the fact. At his cremation, several of his queens and some serving women burned with him on the pyre. This was sati, an old custom in parts of India, in which a widow died on her husband's funeral fire. Histories record it, and Sikh tellings of it are full of sorrow. Second, the Gurus. Long before, Guru Amar Das had spoken plainly. In a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, he says that women who burn themselves with their husbands' bodies are not truly called satis. The true sati, he says, is one who lives on in goodness and contentment, and honors the Lord. The Gurus spoke against the custom, and Sikh tradition remembers Guru Amar Das working to end it among his followers. Third, the gap. So here is a hard thing on this stretch of the path. The kingdom ruled in the Khalsa's name, and yet at its founder's funeral, a practice the Gurus had rejected went ahead. An old custom was stronger, that day, than the Guru's word. Sikh histories say this plainly: the court fell short of the Gurus' teaching. And fourth, what to do with a hard truth. You don't have to make it smaller. You don't have to make it the whole story either. The Maharaja who gave gold to the Harmandir and mercy to his enemies is the same man at whose funeral this happened. Both are true. Holding both is part of telling history with honesty.
screen: `QUEENS AND SERVANTS ON THE PYRE.` · `GURU AMAR DAS HAD SPOKEN AGAINST IT.` · `THE COURT FELL SHORT OF THE GURU.` · `HOLDING A HARD TRUTH.` · then, large: `EVEN KINGS FELL SHORT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a hard truth. Sit, and let the breath be slow and steady. Bring to mind the women who died that day, without names, just as people. Let there be a moment of silence for them. Then, if you like, think of a hard truth in a story you love: your family's, your country's, your own. Don't argue with it. Don't hurry past it. Just let it sit beside what's good, both together. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
His death. The end of the Maharaja's life, and the funeral where queens and servants died on his pyre, against what Guru Amar Das had taught. Today's word.
Your line: even kings fell short. Today, when you see someone you admire fall short, say it plainly, and keep what was good. Day nine hundred twenty-five.

screen: `DAY 925 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TWO HEIRS IN A YEAR.`

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's funeral honestly, and point to Guru Amar Das's hymn rejecting sati as the Gurus' teaching that the court failed to follow.

notes: Sensitive day. Number of queens and serving women deliberately not stated; histories usually give four queens and seven slave girls; confirm 'several' and 'some serving women'.
Strokes in his last years, 'Lion of the Punjab' (Sher-e-Punjab), and giving away treasure in his last days: confirm.

Guru Amar Das, Ang 787 salok, paraphrased: 'not called satis who burn with the bodies of their husbands … satis are those who live in goodness and contentment'; Keeper please check paraphrase and Ang.
'Sikh tradition remembers Guru Amar Das working to end it among his followers': confirm.
'The custom of the courts and the hills' — the queens were partly from hill families; confirm wording is fair.
Year 1839 appears only in the index title; not in voice.

Auditor: 'the custom of the courts and the hills' laid the blame on the hill families of some of the queens (unfair framing); now 'an old custom'.
